newsitem.title: UK: By-election boosts Blair's UK premiership hopes.
newsitem.headline: By-election boosts Blair's UK premiership hopes.

text.p: British opposition leader Tony Blair appeared on the road to power on Friday after a crushing byelection victory over the governing Conservative Party just weeks before a general election.
Labour candidate Ben Chapman romped home in the contest in Wirral South, north-west England, winning a previously safe Conservative fiefdom by a margin of 7,888 votes.
"The public are totally disenchanted with the present government....the people of Wirral have taken the opportunity to say so," said a delighted Chapman.
Prime Minister John Major said he was disappointed by the result, but the by-election had been a "phoney war" and he predicted he would still win a general election.
The Conservatives won Wirral South by 8,183 votes at the general election.
In the by-election, caused by the death of their victor then, Barry Porter, Chapman polled 22,767 votes to Conservative Les Byrom's 14,879 with the minority Liberal Democrats on 4,357.

This gave Labour a 17 percent swing, far more than the 4.3 percent it would need at a general election to win an overall majority in parliament, and in line with national opinion polls putting it some 20 points ahead.

Some 73 percent of Wirral electors cast their votes, a high turn-out which deprived the Conservative of an excuse for a bad result they have often used after by-election disasters -- that their supporters had stayed at home.

But Conservative Party chairman Brian Mawhinney said many people in Wirral had told campaigners they would desert the Conservatives at the by-election, but return to their camp in the general election.
In a statement, Major said: "The by-election is the end of the phoney war. Next time, a cross in the wrong box could mean Britain takes a wrong turning."

He predicted it would become increasingly clear to electors in the next few weeks that a Labour government would mean higher taxes and interest rates. "That is why at the general election we will win," he added.
But Labour leader Tony Blair said: "For Tories to dismiss this as a protest vote simply confirms how out of touch and arrogant they are."

His aides pointed out that no party in Britain's recent history has overcome an electoral deficit of the size the Conservatives now face in the less than nine weeks which probably now remain before a general election.
Recognising that Wirral could presage a huge Labour majority in May, foreign exchange traders sold sterling, pushing the pound down by more than a pfennig against the German mark.
The loss of Wirral South means the Conservatives have just 322 seats in the lower House of Commons, one fewer than Labour and all other parties combined.
Just hours before the result, the Scottish National Party said it would call a vote of no confidence in the government on March 10 and called on other opposition parties to join it.

But Labour deputy leader John Prescott said it would be difficult to force the government into an early election since Northern Ireland's Ulster Unionists had indicated they would not join other opposition parties in censuring Major.
"It will be difficult to defeat the government and we would not be prepared to put a motion down unless we could hopefully win," he said.
Pollsters were proved wrong at the 1992 general election and Major's party is banking on an economic boom and tax cuts to bring voters back to his party.
But all the themes that will feature at the general election were rehearsed at Wirral South, and Major's chances of hauling in Labour look extremely bleak.
